examples.solution_text:
Factor out the constant and identify $a=8$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{4}{\sqrt{64-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=4\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{64-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=4\arcsin\frac{x}{8}+C\end{aligned}$

Here $a=7$. The arctangent primitive requires the factor $\frac{1}{7}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{15}{49+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=15\int\frac{1}{49+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=\frac{15}{7}\arctan\frac{x}{7}+C\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Find $\int\frac{-3}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx$, expressing the answer using inverse cosine.
examples.solution_text:
The negative numerator matches the inverse cosine derivative.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{-3}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=3\int\frac{-1}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=3\arccos\frac{x}{4}+C\end{aligned}$

Factor out the coefficient of $x^{2}$ before matching the standard form.
$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25-16x^{2}}&=4\sqrt{\frac{25}{16}-x^{2}}\end{aligned}$
Here $a=\frac{5}{4}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{2}{\sqrt{25-16x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{25}{16}-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{2}\arcsin\frac{4x}{5}+C\end{aligned}$

(a) The integrand is undefined at $x=4$. Evaluate the convergent improper integral through a limit from below.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\lim_{b\to4^{-}}\left[\arcsin\frac{x}{4}\right]_{0}^{b}\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}-0\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$
(b)
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{4\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{16+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{1}{4}\arctan\frac{x}{4}\right]_{0}^{4\sqrt{3}}\\&=\frac{1}{4}\arctan\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{4}\arctan0\\&=\frac{\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A curve has $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5}{25+x^{2}}$ and passes through $(5,\frac{\pi}{2})$. Find its equation.

examples.solution_text:
Write $1-9x^{6}=1-(3x^{3})^{2}$. For $f(x)=3x^{3}$, the required numerator is $f'(x)=9x^{2}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{5x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-9x^{6}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{5}{9}\int\frac{9x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-(3x^{3})^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{5}{9}\arcsin(3x^{3})+C\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Authored ten worked examples covering every distinct assessed method, with separate editable prompts and solutions, single-dollar maths, continuation gutters and renderer-inherited blue solution ink. examples.derivation: Differentiating 4 arcsin(x/8) gives 4/sqrt(64-x²), confirming the primitive and constant multiplier.
Differentiating 3 arccos(x/4) gives -3/sqrt(16-x²), matching the requested inverse cosine form.
The denominator is 4 sqrt(25/16-x²). The resulting primitive is (1/2) arcsin(4x/5)+C; its derivative is 2/sqrt(25-16x²).
Factoring 25 gives the multiplier (3/25)(5/4)=3/20. Differentiating (3/20) arctan(5x/4) gives 3/(16+25x²).
(a) The interior limit of arcsin(b/4)-arcsin(0) as b approaches 4 from below is π/2. (b) Evaluating (1/4) arctan(x/4) at 4 sqrt(3) and 0 gives π/12.
Integrating the gradient gives y=arctan(x/5)+C. The supplied point gives π/2=π/4+C, so C=π/4. Differentiation recovers 5/(25+x²).
For f(x)=3x³, f'(x)=9x². Multiplying the inverse sine primitive by 5/9 gives derivative 5x²/sqrt(1-9x⁶).
(a) Differentiating (4/3) arctan(x³/3) gives 12x²/(9+x⁶). (b) The primitive is (1/3) arctan(e^(3x)); the endpoint inner values are 3 and 1, giving (1/3) arctan(3)-π/12.

The positive curve has primitive 2 arctan(x/4). Evaluation gives 2(π/3)-2(-π/4)=7π/6 square units. The diagram plots the same curve, shades the requested interval, and places boundary tops at (-4,1/4) and (4 sqrt(3),1/8), consistent with the function.
